newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals -- Japan aluminium premiums seen on rise.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals -- Japan aluminium premiums seen on rise.

text.p: The strong performance of aluminium at the London Metals Exchange and the dollar's decline may push up premiums in Japan for the July-September quarter, despite signs of a slowdown in the country's demand, traders said on Wednesday.
"(The third-quarter) premiums will be a bit higher than those in the second quarter," said a trader at a major trading house. "They'll ask for a hike given the yen's strength."
Aluminium suppliers, traders and large users are to begin talks over third-quarter supply contracts later this week.

Traders said the dollar's fall to below 119 yen from above 123 yen since Friday would help suppliers, who already have the upper hand against a backdrop of lower LME stocks, strong U.S. demand and firm U.S. Midwest premiums.
The strong global fundamentals, coupled with fund buying, pushed up the metal's price in London in the past week and it is expected to head towards a recent peak of $1,707.

An increasing number of traders are worried the premiums might settle above $82 on the long-term contracts for the second quarter, particularly because Japan's sales tax increase has started to bite into the country's economy.
"We've already seen signs for a slowdown in durable goods sectors such as construction and cars," said a second trader.
"Domestic premiums are below those in the second-quarter contracts. We'd like to see a decline."

Aluminium's physical market for deliveries before July remained tight, with premiums at around $85/90 per tonne, traders said. Though the market was quiet ahead of the negotiations, some traders saw offers as high as $90/95.
In the zinc market, premiums eased slightly to $80/85 per tonnes from a previous $85/95 as China was eager to expand exports to cash in on high LME zinc prices, traders said.
"We've got a special situation here: We've just had heavy imports under GSP (Generalised System of Preferences) and we're close to China where they have abundant zinc," said a trader.
"China wants to sell abroad while international prices are high, even at the cost to domestic users."
Another trader agreed, adding that premiums for Japan are likely to fall further due to China's export drive after aluminium rises above $1,300 from around $1,050 early in 1997.

"China wants to sell even if they have to accept lower premiums," the trader said. A rally on LME usually means lower premiums for metal from China as imports from that country are usually set at a fixed price.
A trader at one big Japanese trade house said premiums for some Chinese metal were now as low as $20 a tonne, while premiums in term contracts from other countries were $100.
"As long as the prices remain high, we will continue to see cheap Chinese metals. But China might not press for exports as much as before as its domestic demand is improving."
The physical copper market remained very quiet as users digested heavy GSP imports last month, traders said. Nominal premiums for the metal were unchanged at $60/70 per tonne.
